children: The cost of insuring French government debt against the risk of a default jumped to its highest since March 2020 on Monday, reflecting investor concern about France's long-term finances even as French bonds rebounded after last week's brutal selloff.

Credit default swaps (CDS), a derivative that offers insurance for bondholders, on 5-year French sovereign bonds broke above 45 basis points to its highest since the depths of the COVID crisis, according to LSEG data (FRGV5YUSAC=MG).

French CDS have risen just over 7 bps since last Monday, marking their largest week-on-week jump since June 2024, when a snap election called by President Emmanuel Macron resulted in political stalemate that has kept investors on edge about the sustainability of France's finances ever since.

French 10-year bond yields (FR10YT=RR) on Monday fell 11-bps to around 4.46% as prices rallied, helping bring the country's risk premium over Germany slightly below last week's 14-year highs above 100 bps (DE10FR10=RR).

However, French bonds or OATs are the worst-performing major-economy bonds in 2026, with a rise of over 90 bps this year, compared with an average increase of 75 bps for the broader Group of Seven nations' 10-year borrowing costs.
